title: Silent japa
hookLine: Valmiki's mara-mara; the mantra without the mouth
carry: japa goes inward until it says itself
last: SANDHYA: THE GAYATRI, KEPT AT DAWN.

lines: A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.
WHAT IF YOU CHOSE THE SONG?
cards: You know how a song gets stuck in your head? You didn't decide to hum it. You're brushing your teeth and there it is, playing by itself.
Annoying, when it's an advertising jingle. But what if it were something you'd chosen? Hindu tradition noticed this long ago, and it tells a story about a robber whose mantra started saying itself.

teach.b: Remember Valmiki, the robber from day seven, who sat so long an anthill grew over him? A much-loved later telling says what he was doing in there. The sage gave him a name to repeat: Rama.
But the robber couldn't get it out; the holy name stuck in a mouth used to threats. So the sage said: then say it backwards. Mara.
Say it fast and listen: maramaramara turns into rama, rama, rama. The name was saying itself, and he sat so still the ants built over him. Here's the teaching behind it.
Japa, repeating a sacred name, comes three ways. Out loud, as you did with Hare Krishna, is vachika.

Whispered, lips moving, barely a sound, is upamshu. Silent, only in the mind, is manasika. Many old texts and teachers rank the silent one highest: the quieter it gets, the deeper it goes in, with no sound to lean on.
And past that is ajapa. The a at the front means not: not-repeating. Many yoga teachers say the breath already carries a mantra, a soft so on the in-breath and ham on the out: so-ham, I am that.
You can't force ajapa. You start with silent japa, let go, and listen for it. So when a grandmother's lips move without a sound all the way to the store, she isn't mumbling.

teach.h: JAPA GOES INWARD UNTIL IT SAYS ITSELF.
teach.b: She's on Valmiki's road: from the lips, inward, until the name says itself.

how: Hindu practitioners do japa aloud, whispered or silently in the mind; many meditation lineages teach so-ham (hamsa) with the breath, describing the ajapa japa as the mantra the breath repeats on its own.

o: a mantra that goes on by itself with the breath
a vow to stop chanting mantras for a time
japa said silently, only inside your own mind

games.q: the ways of japa — tap the pairs.

s: in ajapa, you repeat the mantra harder
ajapa means not-repeating: the mantra that goes on by itself. you can only notice it.
many old texts place silent japa highest
the quieter it gets, they say, the deeper it goes in.
the mara-mara story is in Valmiki's own Ramayana
it's a later, much-loved telling; his own epic doesn't tell his robber days.

games.q: you've been saying so-ham silently. you stop on purpose, and after a few breaths you lose it completely. what do you do?
o: start saying it again gently, then let go again.
switch to saying it out loud.
games.why: back and forth. you can't force ajapa; you start silent japa, let go, and come back when you lose it.

practice: Settle into your breath and say your mantra silently, the one that fits or simply so-ham: so as you breathe in, ham as you breathe out, no lips, no whisper.
After a while, stop saying it on purpose and just listen for the so and the ham in the breath. If you lose it, start saying it again, gently, and let go again.

wordCard.voice: Ajapa. Not-repeating. The mantra that goes on by itself, carried on the breath: so on the way in, ham on the way out.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a, not, and japa, repetition: the mantra that says itself.

carryVoice: Keep this one: japa goes inward until it says itself. Valmiki's name turned around on its own. Day one hundred nine.

sources.ref: Dhyanabindu Upanishad (hamsa, the ajapa gayatri, 21,600 breaths)
